questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Circular 230 governs practice before the IRS. Which of the following individuals is subject to Circular 230?

answers.text: Attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, enrolled actuaries, enrolled retirement plan agents, and registered tax return preparers who practice before the IRS — including representing taxpayers, preparing and filing documents, and corresponding with the IRS
Only licensed CPAs who prepare federal income tax returns for compensation
Only enrolled agents, since they are the only practitioners licensed directly by the IRS
Any individual who files their own personal tax return, since self-preparation constitutes practice before the IRS

explanations.a: Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10) governs the practice of attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, enrolled actuaries, enrolled retirement plan agents, and other recognized practitioners before the IRS. 'Practice before the IRS' includes preparing and filing documents, communicating with the IRS on behalf of taxpayers, and representing taxpayers in examinations, appeals, and collection proceedings. All such practitioners must meet Circular 230's standards of conduct.
explanations.b: Circular 230 covers more than just CPAs — it applies to all practitioners who meet the definition of 'practice before the IRS,' including attorneys, enrolled agents, and other authorized representatives.
explanations.c: Enrolled agents hold an IRS-issued credential, but Circular 230 covers multiple categories of practitioners — not only enrolled agents.
explanations.d: Preparing one's own return is not 'practice before the IRS.' The Circular 230 framework applies to compensated representatives and return preparers acting on behalf of others — not to individual self-filers.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under Circular 230 §10.35, a practitioner must possess the necessary competence to engage in practice before the IRS. If a practitioner lacks competence in a particular area of tax law, what must the practitioner do?

answers.text: Acquire the necessary competence by studying the applicable law, associate with a competent practitioner, or refer the client to a competent practitioner — and disclose any limitations to the client
Decline the engagement entirely — Circular 230 prohibits practitioners from taking engagements outside their expertise
Proceed with the engagement without disclosure, using best efforts — Circular 230 does not require competence disclosures
Obtain malpractice insurance before beginning work — Circular 230's competence requirement is satisfied by insurance coverage

explanations.a: Circular 230 §10.35 requires practitioners to possess the necessary competence to engage in practice before the IRS. Competence requires appropriate level of knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation. When competence is lacking, a practitioner must: (1) acquire it by studying the applicable law before beginning; (2) associate with or supervise a competent practitioner; or (3) refer the client to a competent practitioner. The practitioner must disclose any limitations to the client if they proceed.
explanations.b: Circular 230 does not require automatic declination. It permits practitioners to acquire competence before or during an engagement through study or collaboration.
explanations.c: Proceeding without disclosure when competence is lacking violates Circular 230's standards. The practitioner's duty of competence is affirmative — it cannot be waived by simply trying one's best.
explanations.d: Insurance coverage has no bearing on competence under Circular 230. The competence requirement focuses on the practitioner's actual ability to perform the work, not on financial protection from errors.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under Circular 230 §10.29, a practitioner must not represent a client before the IRS if there is a conflict of interest UNLESS

answers.text: The practitioner reasonably believes the representation will not be adversely affected; each affected client gives informed, written consent; and applicable law permits the representation
The conflict is minor and the practitioner believes it will not affect the quality of representation
The practitioner discloses the conflict verbally to each client and proceeds without written consent
The conflict is between two corporate clients — conflicts between businesses do not require consent procedures

explanations.a: Circular 230 §10.29(b) provides a limited exception allowing a practitioner to represent clients with conflicting interests when: (1) the practitioner reasonably believes the representation will not be adversely affected by the conflict; (2) each affected client gives informed, written consent to the representation; and (3) applicable law does not prohibit the representation. All three conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.
explanations.b: Characterizing a conflict as 'minor' does not permit the practitioner to represent conflicting clients without consent. The subjective judgment of severity is insufficient — affirmative written consent is required.
explanations.c: Verbal disclosure without written consent does not satisfy the Circular 230 conflict of interest exception. Written consent is expressly required.
explanations.d: The type of client (individual vs. corporate) is irrelevant to the conflict of interest analysis. Conflicts between any clients — regardless of whether they are individuals or businesses — require the same consent procedure.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under Circular 230 §10.27, which of the following fee arrangements is PERMITTED for a tax practitioner?

answers.text: A fixed fee for preparing a tax return — the fee does not depend on the return's outcome
A contingent fee based on the amount of tax refund obtained from an original return filed with the IRS
A contingent fee for reviewing an original return previously prepared by another firm, charging a percentage of any errors identified
A contingent fee for negotiating a settlement of an IRS examination — the fee equals 25% of the tax savings achieved

explanations.a: A fixed fee for return preparation is permissible — it does not depend on the outcome of the return. Fixed fees (and hourly rates) are standard fee arrangements that comply with Circular 230 because they do not create incentives to take aggressive positions to maximize client results.
explanations.b: Circular 230 §10.27 prohibits contingent fees for preparing an original tax return or amended return unless an exception applies. A fee based on the refund obtained from an original return is a prohibited contingent fee.
explanations.c: Charging a percentage of errors found in a review of an original return is a contingent fee arrangement prohibited under Circular 230. The prohibition covers services related to original returns and refund claims from filing original returns.
explanations.d: Circular 230 §10.27(b)(2) permits contingent fees for services rendered in connection with a matter pending before the IRS — including examinations, appeals, and collection matters. However, this exception applies to representation before the IRS in those proceedings, not to original return preparation. Settling an IRS examination would fall under the permitted exception — but the question must be read carefully to confirm it involves a pending IRS matter.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Circular 230 §10.22 requires practitioners to exercise due diligence in which of the following situations?

answers.text: Only when preparing returns for new clients — existing client relationships eliminate the due diligence requirement
Only in connection with IRS examinations — not in preparing returns

When preparing or assisting in preparing returns, refund claims, and other documents; when determining the correctness of representations to the IRS; and when determining the correctness of oral or written representations to the Treasury Department
Only if the practitioner suspects the client is engaged in tax evasion — due diligence is a fraud-prevention tool only

explanations.a: The due diligence obligation applies universally — there is no exemption for existing clients. Practitioner-client relationships do not reduce the practitioner's professional responsibilities.
explanations.b: Circular 230 §10.22's due diligence requirement extends beyond IRS examinations to all aspects of practice before the IRS, including return preparation.
explanations.c: Circular 230 §10.22 requires practitioners to exercise due diligence when: (1) preparing or assisting in preparing, approving, and filing tax returns, refund claims, and other documents submitted to the IRS or Treasury; (2) determining the correctness of any representation made to a client or the IRS; and (3) determining the accuracy of all oral or written advice given. This broad duty covers every aspect of the practitioner-client relationship and IRS interaction.
explanations.d: Due diligence is a general professional standard — not limited to suspected fraud situations. A practitioner must exercise appropriate care and attention in all representations, regardless of whether fraud is suspected.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under Circular 230 §10.37 (Written Advice Requirements), a practitioner providing written advice on federal tax matters must

answers.text: Base the written advice on reasonable factual and legal assumptions; exercise reasonable reliance on the representations of others; consider all relevant facts; and not rely on representations, statements, or findings known to be incorrect or incomplete
Base the advice on unreasonable assumptions — practitioners may assume all favorable facts to maximize client benefit
Issue the advice only in a formal 'covered opinion' format with all required disclosures — informal advice is prohibited under Circular 230
Guarantee the tax outcome described in the advice — written advice creates a warranty of accuracy

explanations.a: Circular 230 §10.37 sets minimum standards for written advice: (1) The practitioner must base the advice on reasonable factual and legal assumptions; (2) Must exercise reasonable reliance on representations of others, with appropriate diligence; (3) Must consider all relevant facts that the practitioner knows or should know; (4) Must not rely on representations known to be incorrect or incomplete; and (5) The advice must not be marketed or structured to make it difficult to identify the relationship between the advice and the tax benefits discussed. These standards replaced the prior 'covered opinion' rules for most situations.
explanations.b: Unreasonable assumptions are explicitly prohibited. Written advice must be based on facts and law that the practitioner has reasonably assessed — not favorable assumptions that ignore negative facts.
explanations.c: The detailed covered opinion rules were significantly simplified by amendments to Circular 230. Written advice is now subject to the general §10.37 standards rather than prescriptive covered opinion requirements for most advice.
explanations.d: Written tax advice does not create a guarantee or warranty of accuracy. Practitioners can be held to professional standards but do not warrant outcomes — tax law involves uncertainty and the advice reflects the practitioner's professional judgment, not a guaranteed result.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under Circular 230 §10.51, which of the following constitutes disreputable conduct that could subject a practitioner to sanctions?

answers.text: Willfully failing to file a personal tax return when required; being convicted of any federal tax crime; knowingly giving false or misleading information to the IRS or Treasury; and soliciting employment through uninvited direct contact with prospective clients who have not requested representation
Providing a client with a second opinion that differs from advice given by another practitioner
Charging fees the IRS considers excessive for the complexity of the services rendered
Representing a client in a position the practitioner believes has only a 15% chance of success if litigated

explanations.a: Circular 230 §10.51 enumerates specific disreputable conduct including: willfully failing to file personal tax returns or pay taxes; conviction of any criminal offense under the tax laws; giving false or misleading information to the IRS or Treasury; soliciting employment through direct uninvited contact with prospective clients experiencing tax problems; sharing fees with non-practitioners; and assisting suspended or disbarred practitioners in practice before the IRS. These behaviors subject practitioners to discipline ranging from censure to disbarment.
explanations.b: Providing a second opinion is not disreputable conduct — it is a legitimate professional service that clients may seek. Circular 230 does not prohibit alternative professional opinions.
explanations.c: The IRS does not regulate fee amounts under Circular 230 (unlike the AICPA Code, which addresses excessive fees for CPAs). Circular 230's conduct standards do not include fee-level regulation.
explanations.d: Representing a client in a position with a low probability of success is not inherently disreputable — provided the position meets the applicable standard (realistic possibility of being sustained, or not frivolous). Advocacy on behalf of clients, even in difficult positions, is a legitimate professional function.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) can impose which sanctions on a practitioner who violates Circular 230?

answers.text: Only monetary fines — Circular 230 cannot remove a practitioner's license to practice
Criminal prosecution only — violations are referred to the Department of Justice
Censure (public reprimand), suspension from practice before the IRS for a specified period, or disbarment from practice before the IRS — and for monetary penalties for certain violations
Only private letters of admonition — OPR sanctions are never made public to protect practitioner reputations

explanations.a: The OPR has authority beyond monetary fines — it can suspend or disbar practitioners from IRS practice, which can severely impact their ability to serve clients.
explanations.b: Circular 230 violations are administrative matters handled by the OPR — they are not automatically criminal. Criminal prosecution requires referral and a separate process through the Department of Justice. Administrative sanctions under Circular 230 are distinct from criminal penalties.
explanations.c: The OPR can impose the following sanctions under Circular 230 §10.50: (1) Censure — a public statement of reprimand; (2) Suspension — temporary prohibition from practice before the IRS for a specified period; (3) Disbarment — permanent prohibition from practice before the IRS; (4) Monetary penalties for certain enumerated violations (e.g., violations of §10.27 regarding fees). Censure and suspension/disbarment affect the practitioner's ability to represent clients, which is a significant professional consequence.
explanations.d: Censure is a public sanction — it is disclosed publicly, which affects the practitioner's professional reputation. OPR sanctions are not uniformly private.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under AICPA Statement on Standards for Tax Services (SSTS) No. 1, a CPA may recommend a tax return position only if

answers.text: The CPA believes the position has a 'realistic possibility of being sustained on its merits' if challenged, OR is not frivolous and is adequately disclosed — nondisclosed positions require a reasonable basis
The position is supported by a written legal opinion — verbal research is insufficient
The IRS has issued a Revenue Ruling directly supporting the position — only published authority qualifies
The client specifically requests the position and accepts full responsibility — client instructions override professional standards

explanations.a: SSTS No. 1 establishes that a CPA may recommend or take a tax return position if: (1) there is a realistic possibility that the position will be sustained on the merits if challenged by the IRS or courts ('realistic possibility' is defined as approximately a one-in-three or greater chance); OR (2) the position is not frivolous (has some legal or factual basis) and is adequately disclosed on the return. For undisclosed positions not meeting the realistic possibility standard, the CPA should not recommend or take the position.
explanations.b: Written legal opinions are not required for all tax positions. SSTS No. 1 sets a standard based on the realistic possibility of success or adequate disclosure — not on documentation format.
explanations.c: Published IRS authority (Revenue Rulings, Revenue Procedures, etc.) is one type of supporting authority, but SSTS No. 1 does not require IRS-issued guidance. Case law, regulations, treatises, and other sources can support the realistic possibility standard.
explanations.d: Client instructions do not override the CPA's professional obligations. A CPA cannot take a frivolous or improper position simply because the client requests it — doing so would violate SSTS No. 1 and potentially Circular 230 and IRC §6694.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: AICPA SSTS answers to questions on returns
questions.text: Under SSTS No. 2, a CPA should ensure that all questions on a tax return are answered. If a question is unanswered, the CPA should

answers.text: Leave the question blank with no explanation — blank answers are treated as 'not applicable' by the IRS
Answer the question based on the CPA's best estimate, even without client input

Determine whether the question is applicable to the taxpayer; if applicable, make a reasonable effort to obtain the information needed to answer the question; if the answer would be adverse to the client, determine whether the information must be provided
Mark all unanswered questions as 'N/A' regardless of whether they apply to the taxpayer

explanations.a: Leaving applicable questions blank may constitute an incomplete return and could result in penalties. A CPA must evaluate whether each question is applicable and take appropriate action.
explanations.b: A CPA should not fabricate answers without client input. The process requires obtaining the relevant information from the client before answering applicable questions.
explanations.c: SSTS No. 2 requires CPAs to make a reasonable effort to obtain the information needed to answer all applicable questions on a return. If a question is not applicable to the taxpayer, it may be left blank or marked 'N/A.' If a question is applicable but the answer might be adverse to the client (e.g., disclosures about foreign accounts, foreign trusts), the CPA must assess whether the information is legally required to be disclosed and advise the client accordingly. Failure to answer applicable questions can affect the statute of limitations and return completeness.
explanations.d: Marking inapplicable questions as 'N/A' is appropriate — but marking applicable questions as 'N/A' to avoid disclosure is improper and may constitute a misrepresentation on the return.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under SSTS No. 4 (Use of Estimates), when may a CPA use estimates in preparing a tax return?

answers.text: Never — all amounts on a tax return must be exact figures supported by source documents
Whenever the exact amount is unknown, without limitation — CPAs have broad discretion to estimate

When exact data is not available due to unavailability or loss of records, as long as the estimates are reasonable, presented as estimates when required, and obtaining exact information would be impractical — provided the CPA does not imply greater accuracy than exists
Only with prior IRS approval — estimates require written permission from the examining agent

explanations.a: Tax returns sometimes require estimates — for example, when records are lost, destroyed, or unavailable. SSTS No. 4 permits estimates under appropriate circumstances.
explanations.b: CPAs do not have unlimited discretion to estimate. SSTS No. 4 limits the use of estimates to situations where exact data is unavailable and the estimate is reasonable — it is not a license to guess at all figures.
explanations.c: SSTS No. 4 permits a CPA to use estimates in preparing tax returns when: (1) exact data is unavailable (records lost, destroyed, or not maintained); (2) the estimate is reasonable and based on the best information available; (3) obtaining exact information would be impractical under the circumstances; and (4) the CPA does not imply that estimated amounts are exact when this is not the case. Estimated amounts that appear to be exact (e.g., a round number like $5,000 vs. an actual amount of $5,127) may require disclosure to avoid creating a false impression of precision.
explanations.d: IRS prior approval is not required for estimates. CPAs routinely use reasonable estimates in preparing returns without seeking permission from the IRS.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under SSTS No. 6, a CPA discovers that a client has made an error on a previously filed return. What are the CPA's obligations?

answers.text: The CPA must immediately file an amended return on the client's behalf without the client's knowledge or consent
The CPA must notify the IRS directly of the error — the client's consent is not required

The CPA must promptly inform the client of the error and its potential consequences; however, the CPA cannot disclose the error to the IRS without the client's permission unless required by law — the decision to file an amended return rests with the client
The CPA has no obligation to address prior-year errors when engaged only for the current year's return

explanations.a: The CPA cannot file an amended return without the client's consent. The client must authorize any corrective filing — the CPA advises but does not act unilaterally.
explanations.b: The CPA's primary obligation under SSTS No. 6 is to the client — not to the IRS. Without legal compulsion or client consent, the CPA cannot disclose taxpayer information to the IRS. Confidentiality of client information is a foundational professional obligation.
explanations.c: SSTS No. 6 requires the CPA to promptly advise the client of the error and its consequences (including potential penalties and interest). However, the CPA: (1) cannot notify the IRS without client authorization; (2) cannot file an amended return without client consent; (3) must advise the client of the legal requirements (including whether the error may trigger criminal exposure). If the client refuses to correct a material error and the CPA continues the engagement, the CPA must evaluate whether continued association with the client's returns is appropriate.
explanations.d: When a CPA discovers an error in a prior return during the course of a current engagement, SSTS No. 6 creates an affirmative duty to inform the client — regardless of the scope of the current engagement.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: AICPA SSTS form and content of advice
questions.text: Under SSTS No. 7 (Form and Content of Advice to Taxpayers), when is a CPA required to communicate tax advice in writing?

answers.text: Always — all tax advice must be in writing to protect the CPA from liability
Never — oral advice is always sufficient under professional standards

SSTS No. 7 does not require written advice in all circumstances; the CPA should use judgment about the need for writing based on the complexity of the matter, the client's sophistication, and the importance of the advice — written advice is appropriate for significant, complex, or high-stakes matters
Only when the IRS has previously audited the client — post-audit advice must always be in writing

explanations.a: SSTS No. 7 does not require all advice to be in writing. The CPA exercises professional judgment about the appropriate form of communication.
explanations.b: Oral advice is often appropriate, but for significant matters, written advice protects both the CPA and the client and ensures the advice is clearly communicated and documented.
explanations.c: SSTS No. 7 leaves the form of advice to the CPA's professional judgment. Factors to consider include: the complexity of the issue; the client's sophistication and ability to understand the advice; the importance of the transaction; and whether the client needs documentation for business or legal purposes. For routine, simple matters, oral advice may be sufficient. For significant transactions, complex positions, or high-stakes planning, written advice is appropriate to ensure clarity, accuracy, and documentation. The CPA should also follow up oral advice with written confirmation when appropriate.
explanations.d: Prior audit history does not determine whether advice must be in writing. The complexity and significance of the specific advice — not the client's audit history — guide this determination.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: AICPA SSTS departure from prior year positions
questions.text: A CPA prepares a client's return using a different tax treatment for an item than the treatment used in the prior year's return (prepared by a different firm). Under SSTS No. 1, what must the CPA consider?

answers.text: The CPA must use the same position as the prior year — consistency is required under professional standards
The CPA must notify the IRS of the change in position to avoid any implication of fraud

The CPA should evaluate whether the new position meets the applicable standard (realistic possibility or not frivolous with disclosure) independent of what was done in prior years — consistency with prior years is a factor to consider but does not bind the CPA to an incorrect or suboptimal position
The CPA may not change positions unless the client can demonstrate the prior year position was wrong — changes require proof of prior error

explanations.a: Professional standards do not require perpetuating a position simply because a prior preparer used it. If the prior position was incorrect or if a better-supported position is available, the CPA should use the appropriate position.
explanations.b: Changing a tax position between years does not constitute fraud and does not require advance disclosure to the IRS. Position changes are common as tax law evolves or as new analysis identifies a better-supported treatment.
explanations.c: SSTS No. 1 requires the CPA to evaluate each position on its own merits. The fact that the prior preparer used a different position is relevant context but is not binding. The CPA must independently assess whether the new position meets the realistic possibility standard or the not-frivolous-with-disclosure standard. If the new position is better supported than the old one, using it is professionally appropriate. The CPA should also consider whether the change could trigger IRS scrutiny and advise the client accordingly.
explanations.d: Position changes do not require proof that the prior position was wrong. A CPA may adopt a different position that is better supported by current law, changed regulations, or new case law — without requiring the prior preparer to have made an error.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: AICPA SSTS reliance on information furnished
questions.text: Under SSTS No. 3, to what extent may a CPA rely on information furnished by the client when preparing a tax return?

answers.text: The CPA may rely on client-furnished information without audit, as long as the information appears reasonable on its face and is consistent with known facts — but the CPA should not ignore information that appears incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent
The CPA must independently verify all client-provided information — reliance on client representations is never appropriate
The CPA may rely only on information supported by written documentation — oral client representations cannot be used
The CPA may use only information contained in prior-year tax returns — new client-provided data requires audit verification

explanations.a: SSTS No. 3 provides that a CPA may rely on client-provided information without independently auditing or verifying it, provided: (1) the information appears reasonable on its face; (2) it is not inconsistent with other known facts; and (3) the CPA exercises appropriate professional skepticism. The CPA should ask clarifying questions when information seems incomplete or implausible, and should not ignore obvious errors or inconsistencies. This standard balances efficiency (not auditing every number) with professional responsibility (not being willfully blind to red flags).
explanations.b: Requiring independent verification of all client information would make tax preparation impractical and would substitute the CPA's judgment for the client's knowledge of their own financial affairs. SSTS No. 3 allows reasonable reliance.
explanations.c: Oral representations are a legitimate source of information for tax return preparation. The CPA does not need written documentation for every item, though maintaining workpapers documenting the basis for material positions is good practice.
explanations.d: The CPA is not limited to prior-year return data. Client-provided current-year information is the primary basis for return preparation, supplemented by source documents and other supporting information as available.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: AICPA SSTS conflict between advice and return position
questions.text: A CPA provided tax planning advice to a client recommending a specific position. Later, while preparing the client's return, the CPA discovers that recent case law undermines the position. Under SSTS No. 1, what should the CPA do?

answers.text: Take the position as originally advised — prior advice creates a binding commitment to the client
Withdraw from the engagement rather than revise the prior advice

Notify the client of the changed legal landscape; reassess whether the position still meets the applicable standard; if not, advise the client against taking the position or require disclosure if it is still taken with a non-frivolous basis; update the prior advice
File the return using the original position and disclose the case law in an explanatory statement on the return

explanations.a: Prior advice does not create an irrevocable commitment. When circumstances change (new case law, regulation changes, new facts), the CPA must update their assessment and advise the client accordingly.
explanations.b: Withdrawal is an extreme step that may not be necessary. The appropriate first action is to reassess the position and advise the client — not to immediately withdraw.
explanations.c: SSTS No. 1 requires that tax return positions meet the applicable standard at the time the return is filed. When new case law or other authority undermines a previously advised position: (1) The CPA must inform the client of the changed legal environment and its implications; (2) The CPA must reassess whether the position still meets the realistic possibility standard or the not-frivolous-with-disclosure standard; (3) If the position no longer qualifies, the CPA should advise the client against taking it; (4) If the client insists on the position and it meets the lower not-frivolous standard, adequate disclosure should be made. The CPA's professional obligations are ongoing — they extend to the time of filing, not just the time of initial advice.
explanations.d: Filing with the original position and adding a disclosure may be appropriate if the position still meets the not-frivolous standard — but only after first advising the client of the new case law and reassessing the strength of the position.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6694(a), a tax return preparer is subject to a penalty for an understatement of tax due to an 'unreasonable position.' The standard for an 'unreasonable position' is

answers.text: A position that does not have 'substantial authority' supporting it and, for undisclosed positions, does not meet the 'reasonable basis' standard — or for tax shelters, does not have a 'reasonable belief of more likely than not' being sustained
Any position that is ultimately disallowed by the IRS — the standard is based on outcome
Any position with less than a 50% chance of success — positions must be 'more likely than not' to prevail
Any position that departs from prior-year treatment of the same item — consistency is required under §6694

explanations.a: Under §6694(a) (as amended by TRHCA 2007), the standard for an 'unreasonable position' varies by position type: (1) For tax shelters and reportable transactions: the position must have a 'reasonable belief' of being 'more likely than not' sustained on the merits (>50% confidence); (2) For all other positions: the position must have 'substantial authority' if undisclosed; if disclosed on the return, a 'reasonable basis' standard applies (somewhat lower than substantial authority). The §6694(a) penalty equals the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived by the preparer from the return.
explanations.b: The §6694(a) standard is not purely outcome-based. A preparer can take a position that is ultimately disallowed without incurring a §6694(a) penalty, as long as the position had adequate support and met the applicable threshold at the time of filing.
explanations.c: A 'more likely than not' standard applies only to tax shelter and reportable transaction positions — not to all positions on a return.
explanations.d: §6694 is not about consistency with prior years — it addresses the quality of legal and factual support for positions taken on the return being prepared.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: IRC §6694(b) imposes a penalty on a tax return preparer for willful or reckless conduct. What conduct triggers this penalty, and what is the penalty amount?

answers.text: Willful attempt to understate tax liability; reckless or intentional disregard of rules or regulations; penalty = the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income derived from the return
Any error on a return triggers §6694(b) — all understatements are reckless by definition; penalty = $500
Failure to obtain the client's signature on the return; penalty = $50 per failure
Filing the return late; penalty = $100 per day late

explanations.a: §6694(b) applies when a preparer: (1) willfully attempts in any manner to understate the tax liability on a return; or (2) recklessly or intentionally disregards rules or regulations in preparing a return. The penalty is the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer from the return. This is more severe than §6694(a) and reflects deliberate or grossly negligent misconduct — a fundamentally different level of culpability from the unreasonable position standard.
explanations.b: Mere errors or negligent understatements fall under §6694(a) — not §6694(b). The §6694(b) penalty requires willful or reckless conduct, a significantly higher culpability level.
explanations.c: Failure to obtain client signatures is covered by §6695 (miscellaneous preparer penalties) — not §6694(b). The §6694(b) penalty requires willful or reckless understatement of tax.
explanations.d: Late filing penalties apply to taxpayers under §6651 — not to preparers under §6694(b). Preparer penalties relate to the quality and accuracy of the return, not its timeliness.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6695, which of the following is a penalty imposed on a tax return preparer?

answers.text: Failure to include the preparer's Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) on the return — $50 per failure, up to a maximum of $27,000 per year
Failure to answer all questions on the return — $500 per unanswered question
Charging a fee for tax return preparation — preparation fees must be donated to charity under §6695
Using a computer to prepare the return — manual preparation is required under §6695

explanations.a: IRC §6695(b) imposes a $50 penalty (up to $27,000 per calendar year) on a preparer who fails to include a PTIN on a return or claim for refund. Other §6695 penalties include: §6695(a) failure to furnish a copy of the return to the taxpayer ($50/failure, up to $27,000); §6695(c) failure to retain a copy or list of returns prepared ($50/failure); §6695(d) failure to file correct information returns ($50/failure); §6695(e) negotiating a taxpayer's refund check ($500/check); and §6695(f) aiding and abetting understatement of another's tax liability.
explanations.b: There is no §6695 penalty specifically for unanswered questions at a fixed per-question rate. Answer completeness is addressed through professional standards (SSTS No. 2) and general accuracy-related rules.
explanations.c: Charging preparation fees is lawful and common — §6695 does not restrict the charging of fees for services. (Contingent fee restrictions are in Circular 230 §10.27, not §6695.)
explanations.d: Computer preparation of returns is standard and encouraged. §6695 does not require manual preparation.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: IRC §7216 prohibits a tax return preparer from disclosing or using taxpayer tax return information without consent. What is the consequence of an unauthorized disclosure, and what is an exception to this prohibition?

answers.text: Civil penalty of $500 per disclosure; no exceptions — all disclosures require consent
Warning letter on the first violation; penalty only on repeat violations — §7216 has a safe harbor for first-time disclosures
Automatic loss of PTIN without appeal rights; exception for disclosures to state tax authorities

Criminal penalty (misdemeanor) of up to $1,000 fine and/or up to one year imprisonment; exceptions include disclosure pursuant to court order, to Treasury officials, or to other preparers in the same firm assisting with return preparation

explanations.a: §7216 violations are criminal, not merely civil. The civil counterpart is §6713 ($250 per disclosure, up to $10,000 per year). The two provisions work in tandem to provide both civil and criminal sanctions.
explanations.b: §7216 does not include a safe harbor for first-time violations. The criminal penalty can apply to any knowing or reckless unauthorized disclosure.
explanations.c: PTIN revocation is an administrative action — §7216 specifies criminal penalties, not automatic PTIN loss as the primary sanction.
explanations.d: IRC §7216 makes it a criminal offense (misdemeanor) for a tax return preparer to knowingly or recklessly disclose or use for any purpose other than return preparation any information furnished to the preparer for the purpose of preparing a return. Penalty: up to $1,000 fine and/or up to 1 year imprisonment. Exceptions include: (1) disclosures required by court order; (2) disclosures to Treasury officials for compliance or law enforcement; (3) disclosures to another preparer in the same firm assisting with the return; (4) disclosures consented to by the taxpayer in writing (subject to regulatory requirements on the form of consent).

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A CPA prepares a tax return and takes an undisclosed position that lacks substantial authority. The CPA earned $2,000 in fees for preparing the return. The understatement is $10,000. The IRS audits the return and determines the position was unreasonable. What is the §6694(a) penalty?

answers.text: $500 — the §6694(a) penalty is a flat $500
$10,000 — equal to the tax understatement on the return
$5,000 — the minimum penalty under the reckless conduct standard
$1,000 — the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return; 50% of $2,000 = $1,000, which equals the $1,000 minimum

explanations.a: The §6694(a) penalty is not a flat $500 — the prior $250 flat penalty was replaced by the current formula: greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return.
explanations.b: The §6694(a) penalty is not based on the amount of the tax understatement — it is based on the preparer's fees. The understatement amount may be relevant to taxpayer penalties under §6662 but not to the preparer penalty formula.
explanations.c: The $5,000 minimum applies to §6694(b) (willful or reckless conduct) — not §6694(a) (unreasonable position).
explanations.d: §6694(a) penalty = the greater of: (1) $1,000; or (2) 50% of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer from the return or claim for refund with respect to which the penalty is imposed. Income derived = $2,000 preparation fee. 50% × $2,000 = $1,000. Since $1,000 = $1,000, the penalty is $1,000. If the preparation fee had been $500, 50% × $500 = $250 < $1,000 minimum, so the penalty would be $1,000. If the fee had been $3,000, 50% × $3,000 = $1,500 > $1,000, so the penalty would be $1,500.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A promoter assists wealthy clients in establishing an abusive tax shelter, falsely representing that the shelter will generate significant tax deductions. Under IRC §6700, what is the penalty for promoting abusive tax shelters?

answers.text: $1,000 per activity — the same as other minor preparer penalties
Automatic disbarment from practice before the IRS without further proceeding
No penalty — promoting tax shelters is legal and not subject to IRC penalties
The greater of $1,000 or 20% of the gross income derived from the abusive shelter activity — for each occurrence

explanations.a: The §6700 penalty is not a flat $1,000 — it is measured as a percentage of gross income derived from the abusive activity, with a $1,000 floor.
explanations.b: Disbarment from IRS practice is an administrative sanction under Circular 230 — it is not automatically triggered by a §6700 violation, though a conviction or serious violation could lead to OPR disciplinary proceedings separately.
explanations.c: Promoting abusive tax shelters is subject to significant civil and potentially criminal penalties. §6700 is specifically designed to deter abusive shelter promotions.
explanations.d: IRC §6700 imposes a penalty on any person who organizes or participates in promoting an abusive tax shelter — specifically, a plan or arrangement for which the promoter makes a statement about tax benefits knowing (or having reason to know) the statement is false or fraudulent. Penalty: the greater of $1,000 or 20% of the gross income derived from the activity. This applies per activity — each separate promotion can generate a separate penalty. The 20%-of-gross-income measure can be substantial for highly profitable shelter promotions.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Which of the following individuals is a 'tax return preparer' subject to the preparer penalties of IRC §§6694 and 6695?

answers.text: A bookkeeper employed by a company who enters payroll data into the company's accounting system — internal bookkeeping does not constitute tax return preparation
A law firm partner who provides legal advice about a transaction's tax implications but does not prepare the return — advice alone is not preparation
A CPA who prepares only the state tax return for a client — federal preparer penalties do not apply to state return preparers

A CPA who prepares the federal income tax return for a client for compensation — both 'signing' preparers and 'non-signing' preparers who prepare a substantial portion of the return are subject to §6694

explanations.a: An internal bookkeeper entering data into accounting systems is not a 'tax return preparer' under the IRC because they are not preparing a tax return for submission to the IRS. The preparation of the actual tax return by an outside firm or individual would create the preparer relationship.
explanations.b: Providing legal advice about a transaction — without actually preparing or substantially contributing to the preparation of the return — generally does not make the attorney a 'tax return preparer.' The preparation of the actual return document is the key activity.
explanations.c: The federal preparer penalty provisions (§6694, §6695) apply to federal tax returns — not state returns. A CPA preparing only a state return is subject to state-law preparer rules, not the federal penalties described.
explanations.d: Under Reg. §301.7701-15, a 'tax return preparer' includes any person who prepares for compensation (or who employs others to prepare for compensation) any return or claim for refund under the Internal Revenue Code. This includes: (1) 'signing preparers' — the individual who signs the return as the preparer; and (2) 'non-signing preparers' — individuals who prepare a substantial portion of a return but do not sign it (e.g., a junior associate who does the detailed work reviewed and signed by a partner). Both categories are subject to §6694 penalties.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A tax return preparer takes a position on a client's return that lacks 'substantial authority' but has a 'reasonable basis.' To avoid the §6694(a) penalty, what must the preparer do?

answers.text: Nothing additional — a reasonable basis alone is sufficient to avoid all preparer penalties
Obtain a written legal opinion from an attorney confirming the reasonable basis — attorney opinions satisfy §6694(a)

Adequately disclose the position on the return — disclosure on the return (typically via Form 8275 or 8275-R) elevates the protection from penalties when the position has a reasonable basis but lacks substantial authority
Notify the IRS in advance of filing that a controversial position will be taken — prior notification satisfies the disclosure requirement

explanations.a: A 'reasonable basis' alone is not sufficient to avoid §6694(a) for undisclosed positions. For positions without substantial authority, disclosure is required to reduce exposure.
explanations.b: Attorney opinions may help establish the support for a position, but §6694(a) specifically requires 'adequate disclosure' on the return itself — not merely an opinion in the CPA's files.
explanations.c: Under §6694(a), an 'unreasonable position' includes a position that (1) lacks substantial authority and (2) is not adequately disclosed on the return. If the position has at least a 'reasonable basis' (lower than substantial authority but above frivolous), adequate disclosure on the return (typically using Form 8275 for non-tax shelter positions or Form 8275-R for positions contrary to regulations) eliminates the §6694(a) penalty by putting the IRS on notice of the uncertain position. Disclosure does not guarantee the position is sustained — but it removes the preparer penalty exposure.
explanations.d: Prior notification to the IRS before filing is not the correct procedure. Adequate disclosure occurs on the return itself at the time of filing, using the appropriate disclosure form.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6651(a)(1), what is the penalty for failure to file a tax return by the due date (including valid extensions)?

answers.text: 5% of the unpaid tax per month (or fraction of a month) the return is late, up to a maximum of 25% of the unpaid tax
1% of the unpaid tax per month, up to 10% maximum — a fixed dollar amount of $500 is charged at the end
$1,000 flat fee regardless of the amount of unpaid tax
10% of the total tax shown on the return for each month the return is late, up to 50% maximum

explanations.a: IRC §6651(a)(1) imposes a penalty of 5% of the unpaid tax for each month (or fraction thereof) the return is late, with a maximum of 25% (i.e., after 5 months). The penalty is calculated on the net unpaid tax at the due date of the return. If the failure to file is fraudulent, the penalty increases to 15% per month up to 75% maximum. The failure to file penalty is reduced by the failure to pay penalty for the same month.
explanations.b: 1% per month is the failure to pay penalty rate — not the failure to file penalty rate.
explanations.c: The failure to file penalty is percentage-based — not a flat dollar amount. The 5% per month rate ensures the penalty scales with the amount of tax owed.
explanations.d: 10% per month with a 50% maximum is not the correct rate or cap for the failure to file penalty. The correct rates are 5%/month up to 25% (or 15%/month up to 75% for fraudulent failure to file).

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A taxpayer files a timely return but does not pay the $8,000 balance due. Four months later, the taxpayer pays the tax in full. Assuming no extensions, what is the §6651(a)(2) failure to pay penalty?

answers.text: $400 — a flat 5% of the unpaid tax regardless of how many months late

explanations.a: §6651(a)(2) imposes a failure to pay penalty of 0.5% of the unpaid tax per month (or fraction of a month) for which the tax remains unpaid, up to a maximum of 25%. Penalty = 0.5% × $8,000 × 4 months = 0.005 × $8,000 × 4 = $160. Note: if both failure to file AND failure to pay penalties apply in the same month, the failure to file penalty is reduced by the failure to pay penalty for that month — effectively giving a combined rate of 5% rather than 5.5%.
explanations.b: 5% per month is the failure to FILE rate — not the failure to pay rate. The failure to pay rate is 0.5% per month.
explanations.c: A flat 5% of unpaid tax (without monthly accrual) is not the correct calculation. The penalty accrues monthly — the longer the delay, the higher the penalty up to the 25% cap.
explanations.d: 0.25% per month is not the correct rate. The failure to pay rate is 0.5% per month (half a percent), not a quarter percent.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A taxpayer understates income taxes by $15,000. The correct tax liability is $60,000. Under §6662, does a 'substantial understatement of income tax' exist, and what is the penalty?

answers.text: No substantial understatement — the $15,000 understatement is less than 10% of the correct tax
No substantial understatement — $15,000 understatement on a $60,000 liability is only 25%, which is below the 30% threshold
Yes; penalty = $1,500 — 10% of the understatement
Yes, substantial understatement exists; penalty = $3,000 — the understatement ($15,000) exceeds the greater of 10% of correct tax ($6,000) or $5,000; penalty = 20% × $15,000

explanations.a: The substantial understatement test for non-corporate taxpayers: understatement > the greater of 10% of the correct tax OR $5,000. 10% × $60,000 = $6,000; $5,000 threshold. The greater is $6,000. $15,000 > $6,000 — substantial understatement exists.
explanations.b: There is no 30% threshold for individual taxpayers. The tests are 10% of correct tax or $5,000 (whichever is greater) for individuals — not a 30% threshold.
explanations.c: The §6662 accuracy-related penalty is 20% of the understatement — not 10%.
explanations.d: Under §6662(d), a substantial understatement exists for non-corporate taxpayers when the understatement exceeds the greater of: (1) 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return ($60,000 × 10% = $6,000); or (2) $5,000. The $15,000 understatement exceeds both thresholds — substantial understatement exists. The accuracy-related penalty under §6662 = 20% of the portion of the understatement attributable to the substantial understatement = 20% × $15,000 = $3,000.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: The IRS determines that a taxpayer fraudulently understated tax by $50,000. Under IRC §6663, what is the civil fraud penalty?

answers.text: $10,000 — 20% of the fraudulent understatement
$25,000 — 50% of the fraudulent understatement
$50,000 — 100% of the fraudulent understatement
$37,500 — 75% of the fraudulent understatement

explanations.a: 20% is the accuracy-related penalty rate under §6662 — not the civil fraud penalty rate under §6663.
explanations.b: 50% was the former civil fraud penalty rate before TEFRA 1982, which increased it to 75%. The current rate is 75%.
explanations.c: 100% of the understatement is not the civil fraud penalty rate. The 75% rate is specifically prescribed by §6663.
explanations.d: IRC §6663 imposes a civil fraud penalty of 75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud. Penalty = 75% × $50,000 = $37,500. The burden of proof for the civil fraud penalty shifts to the IRS — the IRS must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the underpayment is due to fraud. Unlike the accuracy-related penalty (§6662), §6663 requires intentional wrongdoing. If the IRS proves fraud as to any part of the underpayment, the entire underpayment is treated as fraudulent (burden then shifts to taxpayer to show portion not due to fraud).

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6664, the accuracy-related penalty (§6662) does not apply to any portion of an underpayment if

answers.text: The taxpayer consulted a tax professional at any point during the year
The taxpayer was audited in a prior year and the same position was accepted — prior audit acceptance eliminates all future penalties on the same issue

There was reasonable cause for the underpayment and the taxpayer acted in good faith — based on all facts and circumstances, including adequate disclosure, the legal standard for the position, and the taxpayer's efforts to determine the correct tax
The underpayment is less than $1,000 — the de minimis threshold eliminates all accuracy-related penalties

explanations.a: Merely consulting a tax professional is not automatic protection. The nature, quality, and substance of the advice received — and whether the taxpayer reasonably relied on it — determine whether reasonable cause exists.
explanations.b: Prior audit acceptance of a position is one factor considered in reasonable cause, but it does not automatically eliminate all future penalties on the same issue. Tax law can change, and the IRS may take a different position in later years.
explanations.c: §6664(c) provides that §6662 accuracy-related penalties do not apply if there was reasonable cause for the underpayment and the taxpayer acted in good faith. Factors considered include: the nature of the position (e.g., whether the law was unsettled); whether the taxpayer relied on professional advice in good faith; the extent of the taxpayer's efforts to comply; and whether adequate disclosure was made. Reasonable cause is a facts-and-circumstances determination — there is no bright-line rule.
explanations.d: There is no $1,000 de minimis threshold that eliminates accuracy-related penalties. Penalties apply to the portion of any underpayment attributable to the specified conduct, regardless of amount.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: An individual taxpayer fails to make required quarterly estimated tax payments during the year. Under IRC §6654, the underpayment of estimated tax penalty applies unless the taxpayer meets one of the safe harbors. Which of the following is NOT a safe harbor from the §6654 penalty?

answers.text: Tax liability for the current year is less than $1,000 after subtracting withholding
Withholding and estimated payments equal or exceed 90% of the current-year tax liability
Withholding and estimated payments equal or exceed 100% of the prior-year tax liability (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000)
The taxpayer's total income for the year is less than $75,000 — lower-income taxpayers are exempt from estimated tax requirements

explanations.a: The §6654 safe harbor for less than $1,000 of net tax due (after withholding) is a valid exception — if a taxpayer owes less than $1,000 after withholding, no estimated tax penalty applies.
explanations.b: The 90% of current-year tax liability safe harbor is valid — if cumulative withholding and payments equal at least 90% of the current year's actual tax, the penalty does not apply.
explanations.c: The prior-year tax liability safe harbor (100%, or 110% if prior AGI > $150,000) is valid and commonly used because it allows taxpayers to know their required payment amount at the beginning of the year based on prior-year data.
explanations.d: There is no income-level exemption from estimated tax requirements. The §6654 safe harbors are specific tests related to the amount of tax owed and payments made — not income level. A low-income taxpayer who owes tax and fails to make required payments is subject to the penalty just as higher-income taxpayers are.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: interaction failure to file and failure to pay penalties
questions.text: A taxpayer files a return 3 months late AND fails to pay the balance due. Both the §6651(a)(1) failure to file and §6651(a)(2) failure to pay penalties apply for the same month. How are the two penalties coordinated?

answers.text: Both penalties apply in full — the total penalty is 5% (failure to file) + 0.5% (failure to pay) = 5.5% per month
Only the failure to pay penalty applies — the failure to file penalty is automatically waived after the return is filed
Only the failure to file penalty applies — the failure to pay penalty is waived when failure to file exists

The failure to file penalty is reduced by the amount of the failure to pay penalty for the same month — effectively making the combined rate 5% per month (5% − 0.5% = 4.5% failure to file + 0.5% failure to pay = 5% total)

explanations.a: The two penalties are not simply additive without adjustment. Congress intended the combined maximum in overlapping months to be capped, not doubled.
explanations.b: The failure to file penalty stops accruing once the return is filed. The failure to pay penalty continues to accrue until the tax is paid. However, for the months both applied simultaneously, the coordination rule in §6651(c) applies — the failure to file penalty is reduced by the failure to pay penalty for those months.
explanations.c: The failure to pay penalty is not waived when failure to file also exists. Both penalties apply, but they are coordinated — not stacked additively.
explanations.d: Under §6651(c)(1), the failure to file penalty (5% per month) is reduced by the amount of the failure to pay penalty (0.5% per month) for any month in which both penalties apply. This means: failure to file penalty = 5% − 0.5% = 4.5% per month; plus failure to pay penalty = 0.5% per month; combined = 5% per month. This coordination prevents stacking of penalties to create an effective 5.5% combined monthly rate for months when both apply. After the return is filed, only the failure to pay penalty continues.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A tax return shows an understatement attributable to both negligence and a substantial understatement of income tax. Under §6662, what penalty applies?

answers.text: 40% total — negligence (20%) and substantial understatement (20%) stack additively
40% total — the §6662 penalty doubles when two accuracy-related penalties both apply to the same underpayment
No penalty — multiple overlapping accuracy-related grounds cancel each other out
20% on the portion of the understatement attributable to each separate component — but the accuracy-related penalty cannot exceed 20% of the total understatement for any single underpayment

explanations.a: The accuracy-related penalties do not stack additively within §6662. The total §6662 penalty for any given underpayment is capped at 20% (40% for gross valuation misstatements), regardless of how many accuracy-related grounds apply.
explanations.b: §6662 does not double to 40% merely because two accuracy-related grounds apply. The 40% rate is reserved specifically for gross valuation misstatements (those involving property values or basis overstated by 200%+ or tax underpayment exceeding $5,000 due to listed transactions).
explanations.c: Overlapping accuracy-related grounds do not cancel the penalty — they simply do not multiply it. The 20% penalty applies once.
explanations.d: Under §6662(a), the accuracy-related penalty is 20% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to the specified conduct. §6662(f) prevents the penalty from being imposed more than once on the same underpayment — even if multiple accuracy-related grounds apply to the same portion of the underpayment, the maximum is still 20% for that portion. The penalty is 20% of the underpayment, not 40%.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6501(a), the general statute of limitations for the IRS to assess additional tax is

answers.text: One year from the date the return is filed
Ten years from the date the return is filed — consistent with the collection statute of limitations
Five years from the date of payment of the tax
Three years from the later of: the date the return was filed OR the due date of the return

explanations.a: One year is too short — the general assessment period under §6501(a) is three years.
explanations.b: The 10-year period is the statute of limitations for collection of assessed taxes (§6502) — not for assessment. The assessment period (§6501) is generally 3 years.
explanations.c: Five years is not the general assessment statute of limitations. A 6-year period applies in specific circumstances (substantial omission of income), but not as a general rule.
explanations.d: IRC §6501(a) provides the general rule: the IRS must assess any tax within 3 years after the return is filed. If the return is filed before its due date, the 3-year period begins on the due date (not the early filing date). Example: a 2023 Form 1040 filed on March 1, 2024 (due April 15, 2024) starts the SOL on April 15, 2024 — the IRS has until April 15, 2027 to assess additional tax. This ensures the taxpayer knows the maximum exposure period from the return's due date.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6501(e), the statute of limitations for IRS assessment is extended to 6 years when

answers.text: The taxpayer owes more than $10,000 in back taxes — larger tax debts get extended assessment periods
The return is filed more than 3 months late — late-filed returns receive an automatic 6-year assessment period
The taxpayer fails to attach any required schedules to the return — incomplete returns automatically trigger the 6-year period
A taxpayer omits from gross income an amount exceeding 25% of the gross income reported on the return — the substantial omission rule extends the period to 6 years

explanations.a: The amount of tax owed does not determine the assessment statute of limitations. The extended 6-year period is triggered by the amount of income omitted — not the resulting tax liability.
explanations.b: Late-filed returns do affect when the 3-year SOL clock starts (it starts on the filing date for late returns, not the original due date), but late filing alone does not trigger the 6-year substantial omission exception.
explanations.c: Failure to attach schedules may affect the start of the SOL (the return may not be considered 'filed' if it is substantially incomplete), but it does not automatically trigger a 6-year period. The rule is specifically about omission of income exceeding 25% of reported gross income.
explanations.d: §6501(e)(1) extends the assessment period to 6 years when the taxpayer omits from gross income an amount that exceeds 25% of the gross income stated on the return. Example: if a return reports $200,000 of gross income and the taxpayer omitted $55,000 (which exceeds 25% × $200,000 = $50,000), the 6-year SOL applies. For trade or business income, adequate disclosure on the return can prevent the extended period from applying.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: statute of limitations fraud no limitation
questions.text: Under IRC §6501(c), the statute of limitations for IRS assessment is suspended or eliminated in two specific circumstances. What are they?

answers.text: (1) When the taxpayer is under criminal investigation; (2) when the taxpayer owes more than $100,000
(1) Failure to pay estimated taxes; (2) tax shelter participation — extended to 6 years
(1) When the taxpayer lives outside the United States during the assessment period; (2) when the taxpayer changes their name
(1) A false or fraudulent return filed with intent to evade tax — no statute of limitations applies; (2) failure to file a return — the assessment period does not begin to run if no return is filed

explanations.a: Criminal investigation status and the amount of tax owed do not independently suspend or eliminate the assessment statute of limitations.
explanations.b: Tax shelter participation triggers specific disclosure rules and may extend the assessment period, but it does not eliminate the SOL. Failure to pay estimated taxes is addressed through penalties (§6654) — not through suspension of the assessment period.
explanations.c: Living outside the US can toll (pause) the collection statute of limitations under §6503 — but it does not apply to the assessment SOL under §6501(c).
explanations.d: §6501(c) provides two unlimited assessment periods: (1) False or fraudulent return with intent to evade tax (§6501(c)(1)) — the IRS may assess tax at any time, with no statute of limitations, when the return is fraudulent. The unlimited period reflects the principle that the statute of limitations should not protect those who intentionally deceive the government; (2) Failure to file a return (§6501(c)(3)) — if no return is filed, the assessment period never begins to run. The SOL clock starts only when a return is filed — so a perpetual non-filer faces indefinite exposure to assessment.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6511, a taxpayer who overpaid taxes must file a claim for refund within what time period?

answers.text: One year from the date of payment — refund claims expire quickly
The same period as the assessment statute — 3 years from the due date, extended to 6 years for large overpayments
Five years from the due date of the original return
The later of: 3 years from the date the original return was filed OR 2 years from the date the tax was paid

explanations.a: A one-year period is too short. §6511 provides either 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment — whichever is later.
explanations.b: The refund SOL and assessment SOL are separate provisions with different rules. The refund period (§6511) is not directly tied to the assessment period (§6501).
explanations.c: A 5-year period does not exist for standard refund claims. The lookback periods are 3 years (from filing) or 2 years (from payment).
explanations.d: §6511(a) requires a refund claim to be filed within the later of: (1) 3 years from the date the original return was filed; or (2) 2 years from the date the tax was paid. The 3-year period is the most common — taxpayers filing timely returns generally have until 3 years after filing to claim refunds. If a taxpayer paid taxes but never filed a return (paying through withholding or estimated taxes), the 2-year rule from payment provides a backup period. The amount of the refund is also limited to amounts paid within the lookback period.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A taxpayer and the IRS agree in writing to extend the normal 3-year assessment period. This agreement is accomplished using

answers.text: Form 872 (Consent to Extend the Time to Assess Tax) — a written agreement extending the assessment period for a specified additional period or indefinitely
A letter from the taxpayer's attorney — attorney letters can bind the IRS to extended periods
No written agreement is needed — oral agreements between the IRS and taxpayer are enforceable to extend the SOL
Form 1040X (Amended Return) — filing an amended return automatically extends the assessment statute for 2 additional years

explanations.a: Form 872 (or Form 872-A for open-ended extensions) is the standard IRS consent form used to extend the assessment statute of limitations. Form 872 extends the period to a specific date; Form 872-A extends indefinitely until either party terminates it with a 90-day notice. Extensions are commonly requested during audits to give both the IRS and taxpayer additional time to gather information and negotiate without rushing into Tax Court.
explanations.b: Attorney letters alone are not sufficient to extend the assessment statute. The IRS requires the specific consent form signed by both the IRS and the taxpayer.
explanations.c: Oral agreements to extend the SOL are not enforceable. §6501(c)(4) requires that agreements to extend the assessment period be in writing.
explanations.d: Filing an amended return does not automatically extend the assessment statute. An amended return may restart the 3-year assessment period for items included on the amended return (in some circumstances), but it is not equivalent to a formal SOL extension via Form 872.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A calendar-year individual taxpayer mails a Form 1040 on April 15, and the IRS receives it on April 19. Under the 'mailbox rule' of IRC §7502, what is the filing date for purposes of the statute of limitations?

answers.text: April 19 — the date the IRS actually received the return; IRS receipt is always the filing date
April 15 — the date the return was postmarked; under §7502, a properly postmarked return is deemed filed on the postmark date
April 15 only if the IRS receives the return within 3 days — if received after 3 days, the filing date is the receipt date
April 1 — returns are deemed filed two weeks before the due date under the retroactive safe harbor

explanations.a: IRS receipt date is not always the filing date when §7502 applies. The mailbox rule was specifically enacted to protect taxpayers who timely mail returns that arrive late.
explanations.b: IRC §7502 provides that when a return is mailed before the due date and properly postmarked, the postmark date is treated as the filing date — even if the IRS receives it after the due date. For this return: postmarked April 15 (the due date) → deemed filed April 15 for all statutory purposes, including the start of the 3-year assessment statute. The mailbox rule requires: (1) the mailing must be timely (postmarked on or before the due date); (2) the envelope must be properly addressed; and (3) adequate postage must be prepaid.
explanations.c: There is no 3-day grace period condition in §7502. The mailbox rule applies based on the postmark date — not on how long delivery takes.
explanations.d: No retroactive two-week filing rule exists. The mailbox rule applies from the postmark date on the mailing date.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A taxpayer filed their 2020 Form 1040 on April 15, 2021. On July 1, 2023, the taxpayer files a Form 1040-X (amended return) increasing their tax liability by $5,000. What effect does the amended return have on the statute of limitations for IRS assessment of the amended items?

answers.text: The amended return does not extend the original SOL — the IRS still has until April 15, 2024 (3 years from original filing) to assess any items on the amended return
The amended return starts a new 3-year SOL from July 1, 2023 for all items on the original return
The amended return extends the assessment period by 60 days beyond the normal SOL for the items affected by the amendment — the IRS has until June 14, 2024

The amended return, to the extent it increases the tax liability, starts a new 3-year assessment period from July 1, 2023 for the additional amount shown on the amended return — but the original SOL (April 15, 2024) continues to apply to all other items

explanations.a: An amended return that increases tax liability creates a new assessment window for the additional amounts — the original SOL alone does not protect the additional tax shown on the amended return.
explanations.b: An amended return does not restart the SOL for items that were not changed. The original SOL continues to govern unchanged items.
explanations.c: A 60-day extension is not the standard rule for amended returns. The extended SOL is 3 years from the amended return date for the new amounts.
explanations.d: When a taxpayer files an amended return that increases tax liability: (1) The additional tax reported on the amended return creates a new 3-year assessment period from the date the amended return is filed (July 1, 2023 → July 1, 2026 for the $5,000 additional tax); (2) The original 3-year SOL (April 15, 2024) continues to apply to all other items on the return that were not changed by the amendment. This ensures the IRS has adequate time to examine the newly reported items without giving up the existing assessment window for unchanged items.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: statute of limitations suit for refund timing
questions.text: A taxpayer paid $20,000 in taxes on April 15, 2021. The taxpayer filed a formal claim for refund with the IRS on March 1, 2024. The IRS denied the claim. The taxpayer wishes to file suit in federal District Court. Under IRC §6532, within what period must the suit be filed?

answers.text: Within 3 years of the original tax payment — the same period as the refund claim SOL
Within 2 years after the IRS mails a notice of disallowance of the refund claim, or anytime after 6 months from filing the claim if the IRS has not acted
Within 1 year of the IRS denial — the litigation SOL is shorter than the refund claim SOL
Within 90 days of the IRS denial — the same as the Tax Court petition deadline

explanations.a: The 3-year SOL applies to filing the refund claim (§6511) — not to filing suit after denial. The litigation period is governed by §6532.
explanations.b: IRC §6532(a) provides: a suit in federal District Court or the Court of Federal Claims for a refund must be filed within 2 years after the IRS mails a notice of disallowance (formal denial) of the refund claim. Alternatively, if the IRS has not acted within 6 months after the claim was filed, the taxpayer may file suit without waiting for a denial. The refund route (paying tax, filing claim, suing for refund) differs from the Tax Court route (not paying, receiving 90-day letter, petitioning Tax Court within 90 days).
explanations.c: One year is not the correct litigation period. The §6532(a) window is 2 years from the notice of disallowance.
explanations.d: The 90-day deadline applies to Tax Court petitions after receiving a Notice of Deficiency — not to refund suits in federal District Court or the Court of Federal Claims.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: The IRS conducts three main types of tax return examinations. Which of the following correctly describes all three types?

answers.text: Random, targeted, and voluntary — the IRS selects returns randomly, based on DIF scores, or when taxpayers request an audit
Correspondence, office, and field examinations — differing in scope, location, and complexity
Civil, criminal, and administrative — the IRS uses different procedures depending on whether fraud is suspected
Individual, business, and estate — audits are classified by the type of taxpayer examined

explanations.a: Random, targeted, and voluntary does not describe the administrative categories of IRS examinations. While the IRS does use various selection methods, the examination types are based on how and where the audit is conducted.
explanations.b: The IRS conducts three main types of examinations: (1) Correspondence examination — conducted entirely by mail; the IRS requests specific documents or explanations for a limited number of items (most common type); (2) Office examination — taxpayer meets with an IRS agent at an IRS office; broader review than correspondence audits; (3) Field examination — IRS agent visits the taxpayer's home or business; most comprehensive type, used for complex returns with significant issues. The type selected depends on the complexity and dollar amounts involved.
explanations.c: Civil, criminal, and administrative describe the nature of enforcement actions — not the types of tax examinations. Criminal investigations are conducted by the Criminal Investigation (CI) division and are separate from the standard audit process.
explanations.d: Individual, business, and estate describes taxpayer categories — not audit types. All three taxpayer types can undergo correspondence, office, or field examinations.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: The IRS uses multiple methods to select returns for examination. Which of the following is a primary method used by the IRS to identify returns for audit?

answers.text: Alphabetical selection — the IRS audits taxpayers whose surnames fall in the current year's selected letters

Discriminant Income Function (DIF) scoring — a computer system scores returns based on deductions and credits that deviate from statistical norms; higher DIF scores indicate greater potential for underreporting
Voluntary self-selection — the IRS relies on taxpayers to report themselves when they believe they may have errors
Income level only — only taxpayers with AGI above $1,000,000 are selected for audit

explanations.a: Alphabetical selection is not an IRS audit method. The IRS selects returns based on data and risk factors — not alphabetical order.
explanations.b: The DIF (Discriminant Income Function) system is the IRS's primary computerized selection tool. It scores each return based on statistical analysis of how reported items compare to expected patterns — unusually large deductions, high ratios of expenses to income, or other anomalies relative to similar taxpayers.
