High DIF scores trigger additional manual review, which may lead to audit selection. The IRS also uses: informant tips; related-party examinations; industry compliance initiatives; and random selection for the National Research Program.
explanations.c: There is no voluntary self-selection program. The IRS has its own selection mechanisms — it does not rely on taxpayers to identify themselves for audit.
explanations.d: While higher-income taxpayers face higher audit rates, income level alone does not determine selection. Taxpayers at all income levels may be selected based on DIF scores, related-party connections, or other indicators.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: At the conclusion of an IRS examination, if the taxpayer disagrees with the proposed adjustments, the IRS issues a 30-day letter. What does this letter communicate and what options does the taxpayer have?

answers.text: The 30-day letter is a final assessment of additional tax — the taxpayer must pay within 30 days or face collection action

The 30-day letter notifies the taxpayer of the proposed changes and gives the taxpayer 30 days to: (1) agree and sign the agreement form; (2) request an appeal with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals; or (3) do nothing (which results in the IRS issuing a 90-day letter/statutory notice of deficiency)
The 30-day letter is the statutory notice of deficiency — upon receiving it, the taxpayer must petition Tax Court within 30 days
The 30-day letter is sent only in fraud cases — regular audits use a 90-day letter from the outset

explanations.a: The 30-day letter does not assess tax — it proposes changes and invites the taxpayer to respond. An actual assessment occurs later through the formal assessment process after the taxpayer's rights are fully exercised.
explanations.b: After a field or office examination, if the taxpayer disagrees with the revenue agent's report (RAR), the IRS issues a '30-day letter' (Letter 525 or similar). This letter: (1) explains the proposed adjustments; (2) attaches the RAR; and (3) gives the taxpayer 30 days to respond by: agreeing to the adjustments (signing Form 870); requesting an administrative appeal before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals; or not responding (after which the IRS will issue a statutory notice of deficiency — the '90-day letter' — giving the taxpayer 90 days to petition Tax Court).
explanations.c: The 90-day letter is the statutory notice of deficiency (not the 30-day letter), and the Tax Court petition deadline is 90 days (not 30 days).
explanations.d: The 30-day letter is a standard part of the examination process — it is not limited to fraud cases. Fraud cases may follow a different procedural path involving Criminal Investigation.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: IRS 90-day letter statutory notice of deficiency
questions.text: The IRS issues a statutory notice of deficiency (the '90-day letter') to a taxpayer. What is the significance of this notice, and what must the taxpayer do to challenge it?

answers.text: The 90-day letter is an invitation to negotiate — the taxpayer may respond with a counter-proposal at any time

The 90-day letter notifies the taxpayer that the IRS intends to assess a tax deficiency; the taxpayer must file a petition with the U.S. Tax Court within 90 days (150 days for taxpayers outside the U.S.) to challenge the deficiency without first paying the tax — failing to petition within 90 days allows the IRS to assess and collect the deficiency
The 90-day letter is the final step — upon receipt, the taxpayer must immediately pay or penalties begin accruing at an accelerated rate
The 90-day letter triggers an automatic 90-day moratorium on all collection activity, during which the taxpayer must hire an attorney to appear before the IRS

explanations.a: The 90-day letter is not a negotiation invitation — it is a legal document with a specific, time-sensitive consequence (right to petition Tax Court). Missing the deadline forfeits the right to litigate before paying.
explanations.b: The statutory notice of deficiency (§6212) is a formal legal notice that: (1) informs the taxpayer of a proposed tax deficiency; (2) triggers the taxpayer's right to petition the U.S. Tax Court to challenge the deficiency WITHOUT first paying the tax. This is the critical feature: Tax Court is the only pre-payment forum. The taxpayer must file the Tax Court petition within 90 days of the notice date (150 days for taxpayers whose address is outside the U.S.) — a strict jurisdictional deadline. If no petition is timely filed, the IRS may assess the deficiency and begin collection.
explanations.c: Tax is not immediately due upon receipt of the 90-day letter. The taxpayer has 90 days to petition Tax Court without paying. After the 90 days, if no petition was filed, the IRS assesses the tax and collection can begin.
explanations.d: No automatic moratorium on all collection activity results from the 90-day letter. The letter does prevent assessment during the 90-day period (and while a Tax Court petition is pending) — but other collection on assessed taxes may continue.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A taxpayer who disagrees with an IRS determination has two routes to federal court. How does the Tax Court route differ from the refund route?

answers.text: Tax Court and District Court use the same procedures — the only difference is geographic jurisdiction

In the Tax Court route, the taxpayer petitions Tax Court WITHOUT paying the disputed tax first (must receive a 90-day letter); in the refund route, the taxpayer PAYS the tax, files a refund claim with the IRS, and if denied, sues in federal District Court or the Court of Federal Claims
The Tax Court route requires jury trial; the refund route does not allow juries
Tax Court only handles individual taxpayers; District Court handles businesses and estates

explanations.a: The procedures are different — Tax Court does not require prior payment of the disputed tax, while the refund route requires full payment before suing.
explanations.b: Two distinct litigation paths exist: (1) Tax Court route — the taxpayer receives a Notice of Deficiency (90-day letter) and petitions the U.S. Tax Court within 90 days WITHOUT paying the disputed tax. The burden of proof is generally on the taxpayer. Tax Court is a specialized court and decisions are made by judges (no juries). Decisions can be appealed to the applicable Circuit Court of Appeals; (2) Refund route — the taxpayer pays the full disputed tax, files a formal refund claim with the IRS, and after denial (or 6 months of inaction), files suit in the U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. District Court allows jury trial; Court of Federal Claims does not. Both are generalist federal courts. The burden of proof is on the taxpayer in both forums.
explanations.c: The Tax Court does NOT use juries — it is a specialized court where judges decide cases. The federal District Court route allows for jury trials in tax cases.
explanations.d: Tax Court handles all types of taxpayers — individuals, corporations, partnerships, estates, and trusts — not only individuals.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: A taxpayer requests administrative review by the IRS Independent Office of Appeals after receiving a 30-day letter. What is the role of the Appeals Office, and what ex parte communication restrictions apply?

answers.text: The Appeals Office adjudicates tax disputes as a court — its decisions are binding on both the IRS and the taxpayer without the right to further appeal

The Appeals Office provides a non-judicial forum for resolving tax disputes; it considers the hazards of litigation (risks of losing in court) and may negotiate settlements; ex parte communications between the IRS examination division and the Appeals officer (without the taxpayer's presence) are restricted to prevent bias
The Appeals Office can only confirm the examining agent's findings — it cannot reduce the proposed deficiency
The Appeals Office is part of the examination division and is not independent — taxpayers should go directly to Tax Court to get a fair hearing

explanations.a: The Appeals Office is an administrative body — not a court. Its decisions are not binding in the same manner as judicial decisions, and taxpayers retain the right to litigate in Tax Court or through the refund route after Appeals.
explanations.b: The IRS Independent Office of Appeals (previously called the Appeals Division) provides an administrative forum for taxpayers to dispute IRS examination results before litigation. Its mission is to resolve disputes fairly without litigation. The Appeals officer considers: (1) the hazards of litigation — the realistic probability that the IRS would win or lose if the case went to court; (2) the cost of litigation; and (3) the policy of settling cases where both parties might lose on different issues. Ex parte communications — communications between the IRS examination function and the Appeals officer without the taxpayer's knowledge and participation — are restricted to ensure Appeals remains impartial and to maintain its independence.
explanations.c: The Appeals Office can (and regularly does) reduce proposed deficiencies through negotiated settlements. The hazards-of-litigation analysis often results in middle-ground settlements rather than 100% IRS positions.
explanations.d: The Appeals Office was specifically structured to be independent of the examination function. Its stated mission includes being impartial — taxpayers can receive genuine relief there without going directly to court.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §7121, the IRS and a taxpayer may enter into a closing agreement. What is the effect of a closing agreement?

answers.text: A closing agreement is advisory only — either party may reopen the issue if new information emerges

A closing agreement is final and conclusive on the matters agreed upon, binding on both the IRS and the taxpayer — it cannot be reopened absent fraud, malfeasance, or misrepresentation of a material fact
A closing agreement gives the taxpayer immunity from all future audits for the years covered
A closing agreement is only binding on the taxpayer — the IRS retains the right to reopen the issue within 3 years

explanations.a: Closing agreements under §7121 are final and conclusive — not advisory. Their binding nature is their key feature and the reason taxpayers agree to them.
explanations.b: IRC §7121 authorizes the IRS to enter into written agreements that are final and conclusive with respect to the tax liability for any period. Once signed, a closing agreement: (1) is binding on both the IRS and the taxpayer for the matters agreed upon; (2) cannot be reopened or modified by either party (except in cases of fraud, malfeasance, or misrepresentation of a material fact that induced the agreement); (3) resolves the specific issue or issues permanently. Closing agreements are used to resolve uncertain tax positions, provide certainty for ongoing transactions, or conclude examinations with finality.
explanations.c: Closing agreements do not provide immunity from all future audits. They are binding only for the specific matters and periods covered by the agreement — not for all future tax years.
explanations.d: Closing agreements are binding on both parties — the IRS cannot unilaterally reopen covered issues any more than the taxpayer can.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: In a Tax Court proceeding, who generally bears the burden of proof, and under what circumstances can the burden shift to the IRS?

answers.text: The IRS always bears the burden of proof — the IRS must prove the deficiency, just as a plaintiff must prove a claim
The burden is equally shared between the taxpayer and the IRS in all Tax Court proceedings

The taxpayer generally bears the burden of proof in Tax Court; the burden shifts to the IRS when the taxpayer introduces credible evidence regarding the factual issue, has complied with substantiation requirements, has cooperated with IRS information requests, and meets net worth requirements (for individuals and businesses with net worth under specified limits)
The burden of proof is irrelevant in Tax Court — the judge independently reviews all records without relying on either party's burden

explanations.a: Tax Court procedure differs from most civil litigation — the presumption of correctness generally attaches to the IRS's determination, placing the initial burden on the taxpayer.
explanations.b: The burden is not equally shared. The taxpayer bears the initial burden in most cases, with specific conditions required to shift it to the IRS.
explanations.c: Under §7491, the burden of proof in Tax Court proceedings is generally on the taxpayer — the IRS's determination is presumed correct, and the taxpayer must overcome this presumption. However, the burden shifts to the IRS on any factual issue when: (1) the taxpayer introduces credible evidence regarding that issue; (2) the taxpayer has complied with applicable substantiation requirements; (3) the taxpayer has maintained required records; (4) the taxpayer has cooperated with IRS requests for witnesses, information, documents, and meetings; and (5) the taxpayer is an individual or entity with net worth not exceeding $7 million (for corporations/partnerships). The burden shift is evidence-based — not automatic.
explanations.d: Burden of proof is legally significant in Tax Court — it determines who must produce evidence and who wins if the evidence is evenly balanced. The judge reviews evidence but applies the burden of proof rules.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6321, when does a federal tax lien arise?

answers.text: When the taxpayer files a tax return showing a balance due
When the IRS sends the first collection notice to the taxpayer

When the IRS makes an assessment of tax, sends notice and demand for payment, and the taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay — the lien arises at the time of assessment and attaches to all property and rights to property owned by the taxpayer
When the IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien (NFTL) in the public record — the lien is created by filing, not by assessment

explanations.a: The filing of a return does not itself create a tax lien. The lien requires: (1) a formal assessment; (2) notice and demand; and (3) neglect or refusal to pay.
explanations.b: The lien arises from assessment and non-payment — not from the first collection notice. However, the lien is perfected (made effective against third parties) only when the Notice of Federal Tax Lien is filed.
explanations.c: Under §6321, a federal tax lien arises when three conditions are met: (1) an assessment is made (the IRS formally records the tax liability); (2) notice and demand for payment is sent; and (3) the taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay. The lien attaches to all property and rights to property belonging to the taxpayer at that time and acquired afterward. The lien is secret (valid between the IRS and the taxpayer) from the assessment date but is only valid against purchasers, judgment lien creditors, and mechanic's lienors after the IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien (NFTL) in the public record.
explanations.d: Filing the NFTL perfects the lien against third parties — but the lien itself arises at the time of assessment, not at the time of NFTL filing. Without filing the NFTL, the lien may be subordinate to certain third parties who did not have actual notice.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6330, before the IRS may levy (seize) a taxpayer's property, it must provide

answers.text: A levy notice only to the taxpayer's bank — third parties need not be separately notified
Written notice to the taxpayer at least 30 days before the levy, informing the taxpayer of the right to a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing before the IRS Office of Appeals
Immediate seizure without prior notice — allowing advance notice would permit asset dissipation
A court order from a federal district court before any levy can be executed

explanations.a: The IRS must notify the taxpayer directly — not just the bank or other third party. The Collection Due Process rights belong to the taxpayer.
explanations.b: IRC §6330 requires the IRS to provide the taxpayer with written notice at least 30 days before levying on the taxpayer's property. The notice must inform the taxpayer of: (1) the IRS's intent to levy; (2) the amount owed; (3) the right to request a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals within 30 days; and (4) available collection alternatives (installment agreement, offer in compromise). The CDP hearing is a critical taxpayer protection allowing administrative and judicial review of the collection action before it occurs.
explanations.c: Due process requires advance notice to the taxpayer before seizure of property. Immediate seizure without notice is generally not permitted (with narrow exceptions for situations where collection is in jeopardy).
explanations.d: A court order is not required for a federal tax levy. The IRS has administrative authority to levy without going to court — this distinguishes federal tax collection from private creditors who must sue to collect.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6159, the IRS may enter into an installment agreement allowing a taxpayer to pay taxes over time. Which of the following taxpayers has a right to an installment agreement under the streamlined program?

answers.text: A taxpayer who owes $1,500,000 in back taxes and wants to pay over 10 years

A taxpayer with aggregate unpaid balance of $50,000 or less in tax, penalties, and interest who can pay in full within 72 months — qualifying for the streamlined installment agreement without requiring a financial statement
Any taxpayer who requests an installment agreement — all requests must be granted by statute
A taxpayer who has filed returns on time for the last 5 years — compliance history determines eligibility

explanations.a: A $1,500,000 liability exceeds the streamlined program threshold significantly. Such taxpayers may still negotiate installment agreements but must provide detailed financial information and may not qualify for streamlined processing.
explanations.b: The IRS streamlined installment agreement is available to individual taxpayers with aggregate tax liabilities of $50,000 or less (including tax, penalties, and interest) who can pay in full within 72 months. Taxpayers qualifying for this program do not need to submit a Collection Information Statement (Form 433-A or 433-F) — the IRS accepts the payment plan without requiring detailed financial disclosure. For amounts over $50,000 (up to $250,000), a similar option exists but may require financial statements.
explanations.c: The IRS is not required to grant all installment agreement requests. The IRS has discretion, and agreements must reflect the taxpayer's ability to pay. However, certain categories of taxpayers have expanded rights.
explanations.d: Filing compliance is a factor in installment agreement eligibility, but the primary criteria for the streamlined program are the amount owed and ability to pay within 72 months — not a 5-year compliance history.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §7122, an Offer in Compromise (OIC) allows a taxpayer to settle a tax debt for less than the full amount owed. On which grounds may an OIC be submitted?

answers.text: Only financial hardship — OICs are available only to taxpayers in severe financial distress

(1) Doubt as to collectability — the taxpayer cannot pay the full amount; (2) Doubt as to liability — a genuine dispute exists about whether the tax is actually owed; or (3) Effective tax administration — even if tax is owed and collectible, collection would create inequity or undermine public confidence in the tax system
Only when the taxpayer is in bankruptcy — OICs are available exclusively during bankruptcy proceedings
Any reason the taxpayer believes is fair — the IRS must consider all OIC submissions equally regardless of grounds

explanations.a: Financial hardship alone (doubt as to collectability) is only one of three grounds. The doubt as to liability and effective tax administration grounds also permit OICs in different circumstances.
explanations.b: IRC §7122 and related regulations authorize OICs on three grounds: (1) Doubt as to Collectability (DATC) — the taxpayer's assets and income are insufficient to pay the full liability in a reasonable period; the IRS will accept an amount representing the 'reasonable collection potential'; (2) Doubt as to Liability (DATL) — there is genuine uncertainty whether the assessed tax is correct (similar to filing a refund claim but available even after the refund SOL has passed); (3) Effective Tax Administration (ETA) — the tax is technically collectible but exceptional circumstances (such as severe economic hardship or other special circumstances) make collection inequitable. Each ground requires different substantiation and procedures.
explanations.c: OICs are not limited to bankruptcy situations. In fact, an active bankruptcy case typically prevents OIC processing. OICs are a separate administrative collection alternative.
explanations.d: The IRS does not grant OICs arbitrarily. Each offer must meet specific regulatory criteria, the amount offered must equal or exceed the reasonable collection potential (for DATC offers), and the IRS has discretion to accept or reject based on the applicable standards.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6502, what is the statute of limitations for the IRS to collect an assessed tax through levy or court proceeding?

answers.text: 3 years from assessment — the same as the assessment statute of limitations
6 years from assessment — consistent with the extended assessment period for substantial omissions
10 years from the date of assessment — the IRS must collect within this period or the liability expires, unless the period is tolled or extended by agreement
Indefinitely — once tax is assessed, the IRS can collect without any time limit

explanations.a: 3 years is the assessment SOL (§6501) — not the collection SOL. The collection period is much longer.
explanations.b: 6 years is the extended assessment period for substantial omissions — not the collection SOL.
explanations.c: IRC §6502 provides that after tax has been assessed, the IRS has 10 years from the date of assessment to collect the tax by levy or court proceeding. After 10 years, the tax liability expires and is uncollectible (the IRS must then remove the tax from the taxpayer's account). The 10-year collection period can be extended or tolled by: (1) agreements to extend the period (Form 900); (2) pending offers in compromise or installment agreements; (3) taxpayer absence from the US; (4) bankruptcy; and (5) Collection Due Process hearings.
explanations.d: Tax assessment does not create an indefinite collection right. The 10-year period under §6502 provides a finite window — after which the IRS's collection authority expires for that assessment.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: When the IRS places a taxpayer's account in 'currently not collectible' (CNC) status, what does this mean and what continues to occur?

answers.text: The tax debt is permanently forgiven — CNC status eliminates the liability

Collection activity stops temporarily; however, interest and penalties continue to accrue, the 10-year collection statute continues to run, the IRS may file or maintain a Notice of Federal Tax Lien, and the IRS will review the taxpayer's financial status periodically — if financial circumstances improve, collection may resume
The IRS writes off the tax debt as uncollectible and removes it from the taxpayer's account — the taxpayer receives a credit for the written-off amount
CNC status prevents the IRS from filing a Notice of Federal Tax Lien — the designation protects the taxpayer's credit

explanations.a: CNC status does not eliminate the tax debt. The liability remains in full — only collection enforcement is temporarily suspended.
explanations.b: Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status (also called hardship status) is an administrative determination that a taxpayer's financial situation is so dire that any collection action would leave the taxpayer unable to meet basic living expenses. When placed in CNC: (1) Active collection actions (levies, seizure) stop; (2) Interest and penalties continue to accrue on the unpaid balance; (3) The 10-year collection statute continues to run; (4) The IRS may file or maintain a Notice of Federal Tax Lien; (5) The IRS will periodically review the taxpayer's financial situation (often through review of filed tax returns) — if income increases, the taxpayer may be taken out of CNC status and active collection will resume.
explanations.c: CNC status does not result in a write-off or credit to the taxpayer. The liability remains — the IRS simply suspends enforcement during the hardship period.
explanations.d: CNC status does not prevent NFTL filing. A Notice of Federal Tax Lien protects the government's interest in the taxpayer's assets — the IRS frequently files NFTLs even for taxpayers in CNC status to preserve lien priority.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: The IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien (NFTL) against a taxpayer on June 1. On June 15, a bank files a mortgage lien against the same taxpayer's property. On July 1, a judgment creditor obtains a court judgment lien. What is the priority order among these creditors for the taxpayer's real property?

answers.text: Judgment creditor first; bank second; IRS third — private creditors have priority over government liens
IRS first; bank second; judgment creditor third — the IRS NFTL filed on June 1 takes priority over all later liens; the bank's mortgage (June 15) is prior to the judgment lien (July 1)
All three share equally — federal tax liens do not have priority over private liens
Bank first (purchase money mortgage priority); IRS second; judgment creditor third

explanations.a: Private creditors do not have automatic priority over federal tax liens. Once the IRS files the NFTL, it is valid and prior against all subsequent liens.
explanations.b: Under the 'first in time, first in right' principle of §6323, the priority among these liens follows the filing/attachment dates: (1) IRS — filed NFTL on June 1 (first in time among these three); (2) Bank — mortgage lien filed June 15 (after IRS, before judgment creditor); (3) Judgment creditor — lien filed July 1 (last). Before the IRS files the NFTL, the federal tax lien is not valid against purchasers, holders of security interests, mechanic's lienors, or judgment lien creditors. But once the NFTL is properly filed in the county records, it takes priority over all subsequently filed liens.
explanations.c: Federal tax liens (once the NFTL is filed) do have priority over subsequently filed private liens — this is a fundamental feature of federal tax collection law.
explanations.d: Purchase money mortgage priority (where a mortgage to finance the purchase has priority over prior liens) is a concept in real property law but does not apply here. The bank's mortgage was filed after the IRS NFTL, and no purchase money mortgage priority appears to apply on these facts.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities, and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.text: Under IRC §6672, the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty (TFRP) makes which individuals personally liable for a corporation's failure to remit withheld employment taxes?

answers.text: All shareholders of the corporation — ownership creates responsibility for trust fund taxes
All employees who received wages from the corporation — employees share liability for the taxes withheld from their pay

Any person who is responsible for collecting, accounting for, or paying over the trust fund taxes AND willfully fails to do so — including officers, directors, employees with check-signing authority, and shareholders who control the business finances
Only the corporation's CEO and CFO — only the two highest officers are subject to the TFRP

explanations.a: Ownership alone does not create TFRP liability. The §6672 analysis focuses on who is 'responsible' (had authority and duty) AND 'willful' (knew taxes were due and chose not to pay) — not simply who owns shares.
explanations.b: Employees who received wages are victims of the withheld tax failure, not responsible parties. The TFRP targets those who controlled the business funds and failed to remit the withheld taxes to the IRS.
explanations.c: The TFRP under §6672 applies to any 'responsible person' who 'willfully' fails to collect, account for, or pay over withheld employment taxes. 'Responsible person' is broadly defined: it includes any person with the duty and authority to ensure taxes are paid — officers, directors, partners, employees with check-signing authority, shareholders involved in day-to-day operations, and even outside parties (such as a CPA who controls the checkbook). 'Willful' means the person knew the taxes were due and consciously chose not to pay them (often by paying other creditors first). The penalty equals 100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes (withheld income taxes and employee's share of FICA).
explanations.d: The TFRP is not limited to the CEO and CFO. Any person meeting both the 'responsible' and 'willful' tests — regardless of title — may be personally assessed the TFRP.
